title: Instruments That Decide Where to Look
outline:
Between roughly 2017 and 2023 the job of deciding what phase a sample is in moved, in several experimental communities simultaneously, from a human reading a curve to a network reading raw detector output, and then from a human choosing the next measurement to an algorithm choosing it. Diffraction came first. Autonomy came second, with Gaussian-process surrogate models steering synchrotron and neutron instruments toward the regions of parameter space where a phase boundary actually lives. A parallel thread runs through electron microscopy, where atomically resolved imaging became a stream of machine-readable phase labels and the microscope itself began choosing its targets. Ultracold atoms complete the picture, with transitions extracted from single-shot momentum images.

Built on Park and Sohn on convolutional networks for powder diffraction, Oviedo and Buonassisi on physics-informed augmentation for thin films, Szymanski and Ceder on probabilistic ensembles for multi-phase mixtures, Maffettone and Olds on uncertainty-aware companion agents at a beamline, Noack with Yager, Fukuto and Sethian on Gaussian-process autonomous experimentation with the gpCAM attribution corrected, Kusne's CAMEO, Kalinin and Ziatdinov on scanning transmission electron microscopy, Rem, Köming, Tarnowski and Weitenberg in Nature Physics 15, 917 to 920, and Bohrdt and Demler on quantum gas microscope snapshots.

Leaves open: an instrument that chooses its own measurements is also choosing what will never be measured.

verifiedClaims.claim: A convolutional neural network trained on approximately 150,000 simulated powder X-ray diffraction patterns, treating each pattern as an image rather than as a list of fitted peaks, classified crystal system with 94.99% accuracy, extinction group with 83.83% accuracy and space group with 81.14% accuracy.
verifiedClaims.people: Woon Bae Park, Jiyong Chung, Jaeyoung Jung, Keemin Sohn, Satendra Pal Singh, Myoungho Pyo, Namsoo Shin, Kee-Sun Sohn
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Sejong University and Sunchon National University, Republic of Korea

verifiedClaims.claim: Physics-informed data augmentation of simulated ICSD patterns allowed an all-convolutional neural network to classify 115 experimentally synthesized thin-film metal-halide samples spanning three crystallographic dimensionalities and seven space groups, with cross-validated accuracies of 93% for dimensionality and 89% for space group — demonstrating that XRD phase classification works even when experimental training data is scarce.
verifiedClaims.people: Felipe Oviedo, Zekun Ren, Shijing Sun, Charles Settens, Zhe Liu, Noor Titan Putri Hartono, Savitha Ramasamy, Brian L. DeCost, Siyu I. P. Tian, Giuseppe Romano, Aaron Gilad Kusne, Tonio Buonassisi
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, with NIST and Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology

verifiedClaims.claim: An ensemble convolutional neural network trained on simulated spectra augmented with physics-informed perturbations, combined with a branching algorithm that exploits the network's probabilistic output, automatically identified the set of phases present in multi-phase diffraction spectra — the analysis bottleneck that had blocked fully autonomous inorganic synthesis.
verifiedClaims.people: Nathan J. Szymanski, Christopher J. Bartel, Yan Zeng, Qingsong Tu, Gerbrand Ceder
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of California, Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory

verifiedClaims.claim: The 'crystallography companion agent' (xca) was trained on a physically accurate synthetic dataset and returns probabilistic rather than absolute phase classifications, deliberately avoiding the overconfidence of conventional neural networks so that it can work as a real-time assistant to a beamline scientist rather than as a black-box oracle.
verifiedClaims.people: Phillip M. Maffettone, Lars Banko, Peng Cui, Yury Lysogorskiy, Marc A. Little, Daniel Olds, Alfred Ludwig, Andrew I. Cooper
verifiedClaims.affiliation: National Synchrotron Light Source II, Brookhaven National Laboratory; University of Liverpool; Ruhr University Bochum

verifiedClaims.claim: Deep representation learning applied to large combinatorial X-ray diffraction datasets enabled both low-dimensional visualization of composition-structure space and novelty detection — flagging diffraction patterns that do not correspond to any known phase, which is the practical signature of an undiscovered phase region.
verifiedClaims.people: Lars Banko, Phillip M. Maffettone, Dennis Naujoks, Daniel Olds, Alfred Ludwig
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Ruhr University Bochum and Brookhaven National Laboratory

verifiedClaims.claim: The A-Lab, an autonomous solid-state synthesis laboratory combining robotics, ab initio phase-stability data from the Materials Project, and machine-learned interpretation of X-ray diffraction, produced 41 novel compounds from 58 targets over 17 days of continuous operation; automated XRD phase analysis was the feedback signal that let active learning revise failed synthesis recipes.
verifiedClaims.people: Nathan J. Szymanski, Bernardus Rendy, Yuxing Fei, Rishi E. Kumar, Tanjin He, David Milsted, Matthew J. McDermott, Max Gallant, Ekin Dogus Cubuk, Amil Merchant, Haegyeom Kim, Anubhav Jain, Christopher J. Bartel, Kristin Persson, Yan Zeng, Gerbrand Ceder
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and University of California, Berkeley; Google DeepMind

verifiedClaims.claim: CAMEO (Closed-Loop Autonomous Materials Exploration and Optimization) used Bayesian active learning over synchrotron X-ray diffraction measurements to map a composition-phase diagram on the fly and locate a phase-change memory material with an optimized figure of merit, demonstrating closed-loop autonomous identification of phase boundaries at a light source.
verifiedClaims.people: A. Gilad Kusne, Heshan Yu, Changming Wu, Huairuo Zhang, Jason Hattrick-Simpers, Brian DeCost, Suchismita Sarker, Corey Oses, Cormac Toher, Stefano Curtarolo, Albert V. Davydov, Ritesh Agarwal, Leonid A. Bendersky, Mo Li, Apurva Mehta, Ichiro Takeuchi
verifiedClaims.affiliation: National Institute of Standards and Technology, with University of Maryland and SLAC/SSRL

verifiedClaims.claim: A Kriging (Gaussian process) surrogate model was used to autonomously choose the next measurement point in a synchrotron X-ray scattering experiment, replacing a pre-programmed raster scan with a policy that concentrates measurements where the model is most uncertain — the founding demonstration of autonomous experimentation at NSLS-II.
verifiedClaims.people: Marcus M. Noack, Kevin G. Yager, Masafumi Fukuto, Gregory S. Doerk, Ruipeng Li, James A. Sethian
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (CAMERA) and Brookhaven National Laboratory (NSLS-II, Center for Functional Nanomaterials)

verifiedClaims.claim: Extending Gaussian process autonomous experimentation with inhomogeneous measurement noise and anisotropic kernels made the method robust to the real signal-to-noise structure of synchrotron data, and this machinery was released as the open-source gpCAM package so other facilities could run their own autonomous experiments.
verifiedClaims.people: Marcus M. Noack, Gregory S. Doerk, Ruipeng Li, Jason K. Streit, Richard A. Vaia, Kevin G. Yager, Masafumi Fukuto

verifiedClaims.claim: An autonomous X-ray scattering campaign at NSLS-II discovered previously unknown coexisting and hybrid morphologies in directed self-assembly of block copolymer blends, showing that machine-driven exploration finds structural regimes a human-designed grid scan would have stepped over.

verifiedClaims.claim: K-means clustering combined with Gaussian process regression steered angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy data collection at the Advanced Light Source, autonomously concentrating measurement time on the regions of momentum space where electronic structure features — and therefore electronic phase information — actually vary.

verifiedClaims.claim: Deep kernel learning was run inside a live 4D-STEM experiment so that the microscope itself selected which probe positions to measure next, targeting regions whose diffraction signatures indicated emergent structural behavior — a working automated experiment rather than post-hoc analysis.

verifiedClaims.claim: Artificial neural networks applied to single-shot momentum-space density images from ultracold quantum gases mapped the full two-dimensional topological phase diagram of the Haldane model and gave an improved characterization of the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition in an inhomogeneous Bose-Hubbard system — results the authors state were not obtainable with conventional analysis of the same data.

corrections.claim: The A-Lab produced 41 novel compounds from 58 targets over 17 days of continuous operation, with automated XRD phase analysis as the active-learning feedback signal (Szymanski et al., Nature 624(7990), 86-91, 2023)
corrections.correction: Citation, venue, DOI and all 16 author names verified correct (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w). The problem is stating the novelty count as established fact. Recommended text: 'The A-Lab, an autonomous solid-state synthesis laboratory combining robotics, ab initio phase-stability data from the Materials Project, and machine-learned interpretation of X-ray diffraction, reported 41 successful syntheses from 58 targets over 17 days of continuous operation; automated XRD phase analysis was the feedback signal that let active learning revise failed synthesis recipes. The novelty of those compounds was subsequently disputed: Leeman, Liu, Stiles, Lee, Bhatt, Schoop and Palgrave argued that roughly two-thirds of the claimed successes are likely known, compositionally disordered variants of the predicted ordered compounds (PRX Energy 3(1), 011002, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1103/PRXEnergy.3.011002).' Any book text should attribute the 41-of-58 figure to the authors rather than assert it.

corrections.claim: Extending GP autonomous experimentation with inhomogeneous measurement noise and anisotropic kernels made the method robust to real synchrotron signal-to-noise, and this machinery was released as the open-source gpCAM package (Noack, Doerk, Li, Streit, Vaia, Yager, Fukuto; Sci. Rep. 10, 17663, 2020)
corrections.correction: Bibliographic data all verified correct (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-74394-1), and the first half of the claim matches the abstract. But gpCAM is never named anywhere in this paper — the software attribution is grafted on from elsewhere. Recommended text: 'Extending Gaussian process autonomous experimentation with inhomogeneous measurement noise and anisotropic kernels made the method robust to the real signal-to-noise structure of synchrotron data (Noack et al., Scientific Reports 10, 17663, 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-74394-1). Noack later packaged this class of decision-making machinery as the open-source gpCAM library (https://github.com/lbl-camera/gpCAM), described in Noack et al., Nature Reviews Physics 3, 685-697 (2021), https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-021-00345-y, so other facilities could run their own autonomous experiments.'

corrections.claim: Implicit neural representations were trained to model the dynamical spin structure factor, allowing continuous reconstruction of dynamical correlations from sparse and noisy inelastic neutron scattering measurements instead of binned histograms (Chitturi et al., Nat. Commun. 14, 5852, 2023)
corrections.correction: The citation itself is sound — Nature Communications 14, 5852 (2023), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41378-4, all 19 authors correct and in order (arXiv:2304.03949). The CLAIM misdescribes the paper. It does not perform 'continuous reconstruction of dynamical correlations ... instead of binned histograms'; that contribution appears nowhere in the paper. What the paper actually does is train a neural implicit representation to mimic simulated S(Q,omega) from a model Hamiltonian, then use automatic differentiation through that network to recover unknown Hamiltonian parameters from experimental data. Recommended text: 'A neural implicit representation was trained to reproduce the dynamical structure factor S(Q, omega) computed from a model Hamiltonian, and automatic differentiation through the trained network was used to recover unknown exchange parameters directly from inelastic neutron scattering data on the square-lattice antiferromagnet La2NiO4 — matching conventional analytical fitting without manual peak-finding, and fast enough for near-real-time analysis of multidimensional scattering data.' The affiliation line should also add Howard University (Mardanya, Chowdhury) and Northeastern University (Bansil, Feiguin).
